newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russia govt starts work, Yeltsin meets Clinton.
newsitem.headline: New Russia govt starts work, Yeltsin meets Clinton.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin flies to Helsinki for talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday, leaving his new government to hold its first cabinet meeting and start tackling a deep economic crisis at home.
As the president deals with foreign policy, notably a dispute over NATO expansion in eastern Europe, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin must begin the task of overhauling the economy.
More urgently, he and his new team must try to appease popular discontent ahead of nationwide protests planned for March 27.

The government's communist-led opposition in the State Duma lower house of parliament demanded that Chernomyrdin appear before it on Friday to explain the cabinet changes which left their arch-foe Anatoly Chubais and fellow liberal Boris Nemtsov sharing power as first deputy premiers.

On Thursday, the Duma turns its attention to NATO with a debate which will, for once, allow both government supporters and the opposition to voice a common position, lambasting the Western alliance for planning to invite former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe to become members.

Deputies voted overwhelmingly on Wednesday to debate a non-binding resolution calling on Yeltsin not to allow Russia to join NATO. Neither the Kremlin nor NATO are suggesting any such thing, but the debate will allow the Duma to let off steam.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said in Helsinki that Yeltsin was convinced NATO expansion would be "the West's biggest strategic mistake since the end of the Cold War".
Yeltsin is due in Helsinki on Thursday afternoon. He will meet Clinton in the evening and again on Friday.
Sixteen years older than the American, Yeltsin, 66, is relishing the irony that he is in form after eight months of illness while Clinton will spend the summit in a wheelchair after a knee operation.

Stamping his authority at last on the second term he won last July, Yeltsin dumped conservatives from the government this week, scrapped several Soviet-style economic management ministries and handed sweeping powers to his former aide Chubais, 41, and 37-year-old Nemtsov, a regional governor.
The White House, which will also be talking about bilateral economic ties in Helsinki, has welcomed the changes.
"We may be in a period of real internal dynamic change in Russia," a U.S. spokesman said.

The new Kremlin team will want to show results quickly in the face of mounting discontent, particularly over the failure of officials and employers to pay pensions and wages to millions living on the bread line.

The head of the Federation of Independent Trade Unions said seven million workers would protest on March 27 but side-stepped the question of whether they would maintain their demand for a new government now that the administration line-up had changed.

Revealing a sense of urgency, however, Interfax news agency said Chubais had dropped plans to accompany Yeltsin to Helsinki and would fly instead to the Siberian city of Kemerovo on Thursday to attend a congress of the national coalminers' union.
The miners, who supported Yeltsin in the dying years of the Soviet Union, are now among his most militant critics.
